1. A district has three villages. Village P has 1,000 eligible children with 60% measles vaccination coverage; villages Q and R have 100 eligible children each, both with 95% coverage. Compute the unweighted mean of the three coverages and the district’s true coverage, and explain which weight you used.

Unweighted mean = (60 + 95 + 95) ÷ 3 = 83.3%. This gives the two small villages two-thirds of the say, although they hold only 200 of the 1,200 eligible children.

Coverage is a per-child quantity, so weight each village by its number of eligible children: vaccinated = 0.60 × 1000 + 0.95 × 100 + 0.95 × 100 = 600 + 95 + 95 = 790; district coverage = 790 ÷ 1200 = 65.8%.

The unweighted mean overstates coverage by about 17.5 percentage points. This is total numerator ÷ total denominator, the weighted mean of §2.2.2.

2. A population grew 10% one year and 20% the next. Compute the average annual growth rate with the geometric mean and compare it with the simple average of 10% and 20%.

Growth compounds: the population is multiplied by 1.10 and then by 1.20, a total factor of 1.32. GM = √(1.10 × 1.20) = √1.32 = 1.1489, so average growth is 14.9% per year. Check: 1.1489² = 1.32. The simple average is 15%, and 1.15² = 1.3225 overshoots the true 1.32. The gap is small here because the two rates are close. It widens as the rates differ more (GM ≤ AM, with equality only when all values are equal).

3. An ASHA walks 12 km to a sub-centre at 4 km/h and returns the same 12 km by shared auto at 12 km/h. What is her average speed for the round trip, and which mean gives it directly?

Time out = 12 ÷ 4 = 3 h; time back = 12 ÷ 12 = 1 h. Average speed = 24 km ÷ 4 h = 6 km/h. The distances (the numerators of the speeds) are equal, so the harmonic mean gives it directly: HM = 2 ÷ (1/4 + 1/12) = 2 ÷ (4/12) = 6 km/h. The arithmetic mean, 8 km/h, is wrong because she spends three times as long at the slower speed.

1. Hospital length of stay is right-skewed. In one ward the mean stay is 6.2 days and the median is 4 days. Which would you report as the typical stay, and why could the mean alone mislead?

Report the median, 4 days (with the IQR). A few very long stays pull the mean up to 6.2 days, above what most patients experience: at least half of them stay 4 days or less. The mean remains useful for a different question, total bed-days (mean × number of patients), but it does not describe a typical patient.

2. For a dataset of blood groups (A, B, AB, O), which single measure of central tendency is valid, and why do the other two fail?

Only the mode. Blood group is nominal: its categories have no numeric values to average and no order to find a middle in, so the mean and median are undefined. The mode just reports the commonest category.

3. Haemoglobin of 50 pregnant women at a PHC is grouped as 7 to <9 g/dL (6 women), 9 to <11 (14), 11 to <13 (20) and 13 to <15 (10). Compute the grouped mean, median and mode. Then check the mode against the empirical relation mode ≈ 3 × median − 2 × mean.

Mid-points 8, 10, 12, 14; h = 2; N = 50; cumulative frequencies 6, 20, 40, 50.

Mean = (6×8 + 14×10 + 20×12 + 10×14) ÷ 50 = (48 + 140 + 240 + 140) ÷ 50 = 568 ÷ 50 = 11.36 g/dL.

Median: N/2 = 25 falls in 11 to <13 (cumulative 40). L = 11, cf = 20, f = 20. Median = 11 + [(25 − 20) ÷ 20] × 2 = 11 + 0.5 = 11.5 g/dL.

Mode: modal class 11 to <13 (f₁ = 20), f₀ = 14, f₂ = 10. Mode = 11 + [(20 − 14) ÷ (40 − 14 − 10)] × 2 = 11 + (6 ÷ 16) × 2 = 11.75 g/dL.

Empirical relation: 3 × 11.5 − 2 × 11.36 = 34.5 − 22.72 = 11.78 g/dL, within 0.03 of the formula mode. The order mean < median < mode usually indicates, in single-peaked data, a slight left skew: a longer tail toward low haemoglobin.
